title: Guidance on Using CC Licenses in an AI Ecosystem
content:
Since 2002, Creative Commons (CC) licenses have served as legally enforceable tools for digital sharing. Beyond their functionality, they also signal a commitment to open sharing in the public interest.
CC’s general guidance has been to acknowledge and support all valid uses for each of our current six licenses and two public domain tools.
When making decisions about which CC tool to use, we’ve long encouraged licensors to share their work under the most flexible CC license or tool applicable, while recognizing that some contexts call for added restrictions. This practice fosters robust knowledge and cultural exchange, which in turn strengthens our collective commons. Access to educational, scientific, and cultural content remains essential to society.
However, that guidance was developed for a world of reuse by people, a premise that doesn’t fit as neatly in a world of widespread machine use of content through AI.
So we went back to our own guidance and asked, “Does this still hold up?”
The short answer is: yes.
You might be surprised that this guidance hasn’t substantially changed from what we’ve given in previous resources, even as AI reshapes how content and data is being used.
This full document explains how we got here and contextualizes our guidance for use of existing licenses in this new environment. Our goal is to continue to balance public access with licensor choice, providing options even in this new complex world of sharing. Recognizing that the broader legal, cultural, and technological context will continue to change, we hope this guide serves to clarify and support, in this moment, the valuable educational, cultural, and scientific work that is produced across the globe, every day.
We know that licensing alone cannot address all of the challenges to sharing that AI presents. Our broader work is about finding ways to support agency, attribution, and responsible reuse in a world where content and data can move through systems far beyond the reach of copyright licensing. This means developing new tools and practices while continuing to support a balance of open exchange of knowledge and culture to serve the public interest. CC Signals is one part of that work: a flexible, commons-friendly framework for communicating expectations around AI use of content and data. Just as our existing licenses offer choices between more and fewer rights reserved, CC Signals will offer a spectrum of options for when and how work is used in AI.
We encourage people to share openly using CC licenses and tools to help achieve their goals and values. Open sharing remains essential to the public-interest work of so many. Knowledge and culture are more valuable when people can use, learn from, build on, and share them.
We will be hosting two virtual events to share this updated guidance and how it affects different sectors like Education, Science, and Culture on October 14, 2026. We will start with a short presentation on the guidance and will then take questions from the audience and hear about any feedback you might have.
Register for Session A on October 14 from 9:30–10:30 am EDT with speakers Sarah Hinchliff Pearson, Brigitte Vézina, and Shanna Hollich.
Register for Session B on October 14 from 4–5 pm EDT with speakers Sarah Hinchliff Pearson, Monica Granados, and Shanna Hollich.
Visit the Licensing Guidance page.
Acknowledgments
The Licensing Guidance came together through the work of many across the Creative Commons staff. Special thanks the following team members: Shanna Hollich and Jennryn Wetzler for project management; Sarah Hinchliff Pearson for final synthesis; Dee Harris and Annemarie Eayrs for formatting and publishing support; Diyana Noory, Brigitte Vézina, Anna Tumadóttir, and Timid Robot Zehta for substantial contributions throughout the editing process; and Monica Granados, Taylor Campbell, and Jocelyn Miyara for providing content and guidance throughout.

report.summary: Creative Commons reaffirms its existing CC licenses and public domain tools for AI-era content sharing while developing CC Signals to communicate AI-use expectations.
report.background: Since 2002, Creative Commons licenses have provided legally enforceable tools for digital sharing and signaled a commitment to open public-interest exchange. CC historically encouraged licensors to choose the most flexible applicable license, with added restrictions only when contexts required them, to strengthen the commons. But that guidance assumed reuse primarily by people, not widespread machine use through AI. CC reviewed whether its advice still holds in an AI ecosystem and concluded that it does. The new guidance contextualizes existing licenses, continues balancing public access with licensor choice, and acknowledges that licensing alone cannot solve all AI-related sharing challenges. CC is therefore developing complementary tools and practices, including CC Signals, a flexible framework for communicating expectations around AI use of content and data. Virtual events on October 14, 2026, will explain the guidance for education, science, and culture sectors.
key_points: CC reviewed its pre-AI licensing guidance and concluded it remains valid: licensors should still choose the most flexible license or public domain tool applicable, adding restrictions only where context demands. This approach preserves broad access to educational, scientific, and cultural content while giving creators meaningful choices about how their work is shared.

AI changes the reuse landscape. Training and generative systems move content and data through pipelines far beyond human-scale copyright licensing, making attribution, agency, and responsible reuse difficult to enforce through licenses alone. CC explicitly recognizes that licensing cannot address every challenge posed by AI-driven sharing.

CC Signals will complement existing licenses. It is described as a flexible, commons-friendly framework for communicating expectations about when and how content and data may be used in AI. Like CC licenses, it will offer a spectrum of options between more and fewer rights reserved.

CC will host two virtual events on October 14, 2026, covering how the updated guidance affects education, science, and culture. The sessions will include short presentations followed by audience questions. Speakers include Sarah Hinchliff Pearson, Brigitte Vézina, Shanna Hollich, and Monica Granados.

Open sharing remains central to CC's mission. The organization encourages people to use CC licenses and tools to achieve their goals and values, arguing that knowledge and culture become more valuable when others can use, learn from, build on, and share them. This public-interest framing anchors its AI-era guidance.
report.impact: For the AI industry, CC's position means openly licensed content can still be used for training and other AI purposes under existing license terms, but companies should expect growing expectations around attribution, AI-use signaling, and responsible data governance. Developers should track license obligations and emerging metadata frameworks such as CC Signals instead of assuming that open content is unrestricted. For creators and regular users, CC licenses remain a familiar way to share while retaining choices, and CC Signals may eventually provide clearer controls over AI reuse. However, because licensing alone cannot govern all AI workflows, legal, ethical, and sector-specific debates will continue, and organizations should prepare for evolving norms, documentation practices, and compliance expectations.
report.tools: Watch Creative Commons' CC Signals framework, which aims to express AI-use preferences alongside CC licenses. Use the CC License Chooser to select appropriate sharing terms, and review CC's updated licensing guidance for education, science, and culture. For open-source and data-sharing projects, monitor emerging AI-use metadata standards and provenance tools that help developers document permissions, attribution, and license compatibility across AI training and deployment pipelines.
